rounds.what_returned: Immediately returned Snopes, Full Fact, Lead Stories, and Politifact fact-checks directly addressing this exact claim. All four major fact-checkers rate the claim false. Also returned the original Pfizer document on archive.org and phmpt.org.
rounds.lesson: The claim is a recurring one — first went viral in 2022 and resurfaced in May 2026 with hantavirus as the hook. Searching 'hantavirus COVID vaccine side effect fact check' surfaces the most relevant results instantly. The 'monitoring list explained' angle also works well.

rounds.what_returned: Snopes returned 402 (paywalled). Lead Stories confirmed: hantavirus appears in the 'adverse events of special interest' (AESI) list — conditions compiled by Brighton Collaboration, EMA, CDC, and UK regulators to monitor during rollout, not confirmed side effects. Full Fact confirmed: False verdict, AESI ≠ side effects. Politifact confirmed: False, 'inclusion does not necessarily signal causality', document explicitly says so.
rounds.lesson: Full Fact and Lead Stories are the most reliably fetchable. Politifact also fully accessible. Snopes paywalled but its verdict was clear from the search snippet.

found_sources.what_it_establishes: Hantavirus appears in the AESI (adverse events of special interest) surveillance list — conditions that Brighton Collaboration, EMA, CDC, and MHRA required Pfizer to monitor. It does not appear in the list of events that actually occurred in vaccinated people. The document itself states 'inclusion does not necessarily signal causality.'

insights.would_multipass_help: no — Round 1 queries immediately surfaced 4+ authoritative fact-checkers. This is a well-documented false claim with abundant fact-check coverage. A second pass would add no meaningful sources.
insights.deepseek_advice: For tweets showing a list of medical conditions from an official-looking document and claiming the list = vaccine side effects, the gold query pattern is: '[condition name] COVID vaccine side effect fact check'. The 5.3.6 document claim is a recurring one — searching the document section number plus 'adverse events of special interest' also works well. Always distinguish between surveillance/monitoring lists (AESI) and confirmed adverse reactions in the correction.
